objective: Build and compare linear cost models, distinguish revenue from profit, and make defensible decisions when quantities must be whole numbers.
instructions: Finish four chapters in order: learn a new move, check a guided example, practice, and solve an independent checkpoint. Record your reasoning to recover each broadcast fragment. Finish a five-question mastery check and export your report.
opening: The Equation Vault opens. Your rover rolls out carrying an old memory card labeled SIGNAL ZERO. At Meridian Middle’s student-run Night Market, the robotics club is rehearsing an approved projection show. But the card contains an unfinished broadcast: “If you can hear this, follow the numbers. The missing part is…” Then static. Your team—Maya, the designer; Eli, the sound tech; and you, the analyst—has one afternoon to fund a replacement data receiver. The story is fictional; all prices are simplified classroom models with no tax, discounts, or unsold inventory.

stages.title: The receipt nobody signed
stages.story: A faded receipt lists two badge-printing services. The club will sell the badges to fund the receiver. Service A charges $36 once, plus $1.50 per badge. Service B charges $12 once, plus $3 per badge. A handwritten note says, “The cheapest setup is not always the cheapest mission.”
teach: A fixed cost happens once. A variable cost changes with the quantity. For n badges, A(n) = 36 + 1.50n and B(n) = 12 + 3n. Both are total costs in dollars, not prices per badge.
The input n is a nonnegative whole number. Keep the units attached: dollars per badge × badges = dollars. Multiplication happens before addition.
A model can run forward to predict a total or backward to recover a missing quantity. This extends the Vault’s equations into interpreting real receipts.
worked: Different example: a sticker order costs $18 setup plus $2.50 per sheet. Let s be whole sheets. C(s) = 18 + 2.50s.
For 12 sheets, C(12) = 18 + 2.50(12) = $48. The setup fee is charged once.
If the bill is $63, solve 18 + 2.50s = 63. Subtract 18, then divide by 2.50: s = 18 sheets.
Check: 18 + 2.50(18) = 63. The answer is a quantity, so include sheets.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives Service A’s TOTAL cost for n badges?
questions.hint: Separate the one-time fee from the per-badge cost.
questions.explanation: The $36 fee is fixed; $1.50 is multiplied by the number of badges.

questions.prompt: The club orders 20 badges from A. What is the total cost, in dollars?
An A receipt totals $81. How many badges were ordered?

stages.reflection: Explain how you separated the fixed and variable costs, and how you checked the recovered badge count.
stages.reveal: The receipt’s back has a stamp: MERIDIAN ARCHIVE — STUDENT COPY. Maya recognizes the logo from an old school art club. The broadcast might be a message left by students, not a broken announcement.

stages.title: The crossover clue
stages.story: Eli wants B because its setup fee is lower. Maya wants A because its badge rate is lower. Neither has considered how many badges the club will actually order. The next fragment unlocks only after your team settles the disagreement with evidence.
teach: A break-even point tells when totals are equal. It does not tell which choice is better for every quantity. Compare both sides of the crossover.
For A and B, set 36 + 1.50n = 12 + 3n. Then 24 = 1.50n, so n = 16. At 16 badges both cost $60.
Below 16, B is cheaper. Above 16, A is cheaper. A table connects an equation to a decision; compare TOTAL costs at the same input.
worked: Different rental example: X = 20 + 4h and Y = 8 + 6h, with h hours.
Set totals equal: 20 + 4h = 8 + 6h. Then 12 = 2h, so h = 6. Both cost $44.
At h = 2: X = $28 and Y = $20, so Y wins. At h = 10: X = $60 and Y = $68, so X wins.
State the condition: choose Y for fewer than 6 hours, either at 6, X for more than 6.

table.caption: Badge total costs — same quantity, two services

questions.prompt: At how many badges do A and B have equal total costs?
questions.explanation: The fixed-cost difference is $24 and the rate difference is $1.50 per badge. 24 ÷ 1.50 = 16 badges.

questions.prompt: The club needs 24 badges. Which recommendation is supported by the table?

choices.text: Choose A: $72 versus B’s $84.
Choose B because its setup fee is lower.
Either: they always cost the same.

questions.hint: Compare both totals at n = 24, rather than comparing only fees.
questions.explanation: A costs $72, B costs $84. A saves $12 for this order.

questions.prompt: Which rule is valid for every nonnegative whole-number badge order?

choices.text: B below 16 badges; either at 16; A above 16.
A below 16; either at 16; B above 16.
A is always cheaper because its rate is lower.

questions.explanation: B’s lower setup wins below the crossover. A’s lower rate wins above it. At n = 16 both cost $60.

stages.reflection: Use a quantity below the crossover and a quantity above it to explain why a single “always cheaper” claim fails.
stages.reveal: At the crossover point, the recovered audio says: “We saved the first half in plain sight. The second half is for the people who come after us.” The archive date is seven years old. Someone planned a future audience.

stages.title: The money that is not yours yet
stages.story: The club chooses A for its planned order. Each badge sells for $5. Eli sees $120 of sales from 24 badges and calls it $120 earned. Maya points to the printing bill. The receiver costs money; the team needs the amount left AFTER costs.
teach: Revenue is money collected from sales. Cost is money spent. Profit is revenue minus cost. A negative profit is a loss.
If every ordered badge sells for $5, R(n) = 5n. With A, C(n) = 36 + 1.50n. Therefore P(n) = 5n − (36 + 1.50n) = 3.50n − 36.
The parentheses matter: subtract BOTH the setup and variable cost. The contribution of one extra sold badge is $3.50 after its printing cost. This is the new skill of building a net-change model.
Our model assumes every ordered badge sells. If some remain unsold, revenue depends on badges SOLD while cost depends on badges PRINTED; one n would no longer describe both quantities.
worked: Different example: keychains sell for $6 each and cost $20 setup plus $2 per keychain. Assume every keychain sells.
At k = 3, P = 12 − 20 = −$8: the project has not yet recovered its setup cost.
At k = 9, P = 36 − 20 = $16. Check separately: revenue $54 minus cost $38 = $16.

questions.prompt: Which expression is the badge project’s PROFIT if every printed badge sells?

choices.text: 5n

questions.hint: Start with sales money, then subtract the entire cost.

questions.prompt: All 20 badges sell. What is profit in dollars?
The receiver needs exactly $69 of profit. Under this model, how many badges must be printed AND sold?
questions.explanation: 3.50n − 36 = 69 gives 3.50n = 105, so n = 30. Revenue $150 minus cost $81 leaves $69.

stages.reflection: Explain why sales revenue alone cannot pay for the receiver, and state the assumption that lets one variable model both printing and sales.
stages.reveal: The receiver starts. A waveform appears: not an emergency signal, but a student-made music track with gaps. Beneath it is a filename: TO_NEXT_YEAR_FINAL_FINAL_v7. Maya laughs: “That is definitely a student file.”

stages.title: The fraction on the invoice
stages.story: The replacement cable adds $8, so the team now needs at least $77 profit. Solving for exactly $77 gives a fractional badge count. You cannot print part of a badge. This last checkpoint tests whether you can turn algebra into a decision someone could actually use.
teach: An algebraic threshold may lie between whole-number quantities. Interpret it using the context and verify the neighboring whole numbers.
For at least $77 profit, the equality boundary is 3.50n − 36 = 77, giving n = 113/3.5 ≈ 32.29. This is a boundary, not a usable badge order.
At 32 badges profit is $76, too little. At 33 it is $79.50, enough. The smallest workable count is 33; always test the adjacent integers.
Do not blindly round to the nearest integer. Rounding 32.29 to 32 would miss the goal. The next mission will express “at least” with an inequality and describe ALL workable quantities.
worked: Different example: a stand earns P(k) = 4k − 15 dollars and needs at least $30 profit.
11 items give $29, which misses $30. 12 items give $33, which meets it.
The minimum usable count is 12. If the task instead capped a resource, the direction of the decision could change.

questions.prompt: Why is 32 badges not enough for the $77 target?

choices.text: Profit is $76, which is $1 short.
It is enough because 32.29 rounds to 32.
32 badges cost $77 exactly.

questions.explanation: 32 badges produce $76 profit. A target is met by checking the quantity, not by ordinary rounding.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest whole-number badge count that yields at least $77 profit?
questions.explanation: 32 gives $76; 33 gives $79.50. The minimum is 33 badges.

questions.prompt: The team prints 33 badges but sells only 28. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Profit is 5(28) − [36 + 1.50(33)] = $54.50, so the $77 goal is missed.
Use P(33) = $79.50 because printed badges count as sales.
Profit is 5(28) = $140; printing costs no longer matter.

questions.explanation: Revenue is $140 from 28 sales. Printing cost is $85.50 for 33 badges. Profit is $54.50. The all-sell assumption matters.

stages.reflection: Defend the minimum whole-number order for the target, then explain how unsold inventory changes the model.
stages.reveal: The receiver decodes: “This is not a rescue call. It is a handoff. Meet us at the SIGNAL WINDOW.” The next file lists a budget cap, a minimum runtime, and a battery reserve. Equalities found the boundaries. To hear the whole message, your team must find the possibilities BETWEEN them.

forms.prompt: A new printer charges $24 setup plus $2 per badge. What is the total cost for 18 badges?
Compare X = 24 + 2n and Y = 6 + 3n. At how many badges are the totals equal?
For 30 badges, which printer is cheaper: X = 24 + 2n or Y = 6 + 3n?

choices.text: X: $84, versus Y’s $96.
Y, because its setup fee is lower.
They are equal at every quantity.

forms.explanation: At n = 30, X is $84 and Y is $96.

forms.prompt: Badges sell for $5 each. Cost is 24 + 2n. If all 20 printed badges sell, what is profit?
forms.explanation: Revenue is $100 and cost is $64, leaving $36.

forms.prompt: Using profit P(n) = 3n − 24, what is the minimum whole number sold to earn at least $50 profit?
forms.explanation: The threshold is 74/3 ≈ 24.67. 24 gives $48; 25 gives $51, so 25 is the minimum.

forms.prompt: A new printer charges $28 setup plus $1.50 per badge. What is the total for 16 badges?
Compare X = 28 + 1.50n and Y = 8 + 2.50n. At how many badges are costs equal?
At 30 badges, which is cheaper: X = 28 + 1.50n or Y = 8 + 2.50n?

choices.text: X: $73 versus Y’s $83.
Y, since its fixed fee is lower.
Both cost $58 at 30 badges.

forms.explanation: X(30) = $73; Y(30) = $83. $58 is their cost at 20 badges.

forms.prompt: Each badge sells for $5.50; cost is 28 + 1.50n. All 18 printed badges sell. What is profit?
forms.explanation: Revenue is $99; cost is $55; profit is $44.

forms.prompt: Profit is P(n) = 4n − 28. What is the minimum whole-number count for at least $45 profit?

ending: You have funded the receiver on paper and recovered the first half of the broadcast. The voice belongs to an earlier Meridian student crew. They hid a record of ordinary school life—inside jokes, art, and music—in a time-capsule broadcast. But its last segment only plays inside a valid “signal window.” Your next job is to plan a showcase session that meets every limit.
reportPrompt: Recommend a badge plan and a whole-number sales target. Use cost, revenue, profit, and one limitation of the model to defend your decision.
